title: High School Mathematics
subtitle: From equations to probability
description: A 14-lesson course built for live teaching: short notes, worked examples, auto-checked practice and quick quizzes. Teach it in a Signal Classroom or let students study alone.
note: Topics are grouped for clarity. Check the order against your own national syllabus and adjust as needed.

lessons.title: Solving linear equations
goals: Solve equations with one unknown using inverse operations
Expand brackets and collect like terms
Check a solution by substituting it back
notes: An equation is a balance. Whatever you do to one side, you must do to the other.

list: Collect the x-terms on one side and the numbers on the other.
Divide by the coefficient of x.
Check by substituting your answer back.

notes.f: ax + b = c   →   x = (c − b) / a

examples.q: Solve 3x + 5 = 20
Solve 2(x − 3) = 4x + 2

practice.q: Solve 5x − 7 = 18. What is x?
Solve 3(x + 2) = 2x + 11. What is x?
Solve x/4 + 3 = 8. What is x?
Solve 7 − 2x = 1. What is x?

quiz.q: What is the best first step to solve 2x + 6 = 14?
quiz.why: Undo the +6 by subtracting 6 from both sides, giving 2x = 8.

lessons.tip: Have students say each step aloud ("I subtract 6 from both sides"). It builds the balance habit.

lessons.title: Inequalities
goals: Solve linear inequalities
Flip the sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative
Describe solutions on a number line
notes: An inequality compares two expressions using <, >, ≤ or ≥. It usually has infinitely many solutions.
Solve it like an equation, but when you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, reverse the inequality sign.

list: Open circle: the endpoint is not included (< or >).
Closed circle: the endpoint is included (≤ or ≥).

examples.q: Solve 3x − 4 ≥ 11
examples.a: x ≥ 5 (closed circle at 5, arrow to the right)

examples.q: Solve −2x < 8
steps: Divide by −2 and flip the sign: x > −4

practice.q: What is the largest integer that satisfies 2x + 3 < 11?
practice.sol: 2x < 8, so x < 4. The largest integer is 3.

practice.q: What is the smallest integer that satisfies 5x − 2 ≥ 13?
What is the smallest integer that satisfies −3x ≤ 12?
practice.sol: Divide by −3 and flip the sign: x ≥ −4.

practice.q: How many positive integers satisfy x + 4 < 9?

quiz.why: Multiply by −1 and flip the sign: x < −3.
At least means greater than or equal to.

lessons.tip: Test one number from your solution set in the original inequality to confirm the direction.

lessons.title: Systems of linear equations
goals: Solve two equations with two unknowns
Choose between substitution and elimination
Build a system from a word problem
notes: A system has two equations and two unknowns. The solution is the point where the two lines cross.
Add or subtract the equations so that one variable disappears.
Write one variable in terms of the other, then substitute it into the second equation.

notes.f: x + y = 10 and x − y = 2   →   add: 2x = 12

examples.q: Solve x + y = 10 and x − y = 2
Solve y = 2x − 1 and 3x + y = 14

practice.q: Solve x + y = 7 and x − y = 1. What is x?
Solve 2x + y = 11 and x − y = 1. What is y?
Solve y = 3x and x + y = 20. What is y?
Two adult tickets and three child tickets cost 190 birr. One adult and one child ticket cost 70 birr. What does one child ticket cost (birr)?
practice.sol: a + c = 70 and 2a + 3c = 190. Substitute a = 70 − c: 140 + c = 190, so c = 50.
practice.hint: Let a = adult price and c = child price.

quiz.q: Which method is quickest for x + y = 9 and x − y = 3?
quiz.why: The y-terms are opposites, so adding removes y immediately.

quiz.q: Two parallel lines form a system with...
quiz.why: Parallel lines never meet.

lessons.tip: Ask students to check their answer in both original equations, not just one.

lessons.title: Factorising and solving quadratics
goals: Factorise x² + bx + c
Use the zero-product property
Solve quadratic equations by factorising
notes: A quadratic equation has the form ax² + bx + c = 0.
Find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b.

notes.f: x² + bx + c = (x + p)(x + q)   where pq = c and p + q = b

notes: If A × B = 0, then A = 0 or B = 0.

examples.q: Solve x² + 5x + 6 = 0
steps: Two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to 5: 2 and 3

examples.q: Solve x² − x − 12 = 0
steps: Multiply to −12 and add to −1: −4 and 3

practice.q: Solve x² − 7x + 12 = 0. What is the larger root?
Solve x² + 2x − 15 = 0. What is the positive root?
Solve x² − 9 = 0. What is the positive root?
Solve x² = 5x. What is the non-zero root?
practice.sol: x² − 5x = 0, so x(x − 5) = 0. Never divide by x: you would lose the root x = 0.

quiz.why: Set each factor to zero: x = 2 or x = −6.

lessons.tip: Always make one side zero before factorising.

lessons.title: The quadratic formula and the discriminant
goals: Use the quadratic formula
Compute the discriminant
Decide how many real roots a quadratic has
notes: Not every quadratic factorises neatly. The quadratic formula always works.

list: Δ < 0: no real roots (the parabola misses the x-axis)

examples.q: Solve 2x² + 3x − 2 = 0
How many real roots does x² + 2x + 5 = 0 have?

practice.q: Find the discriminant of x² − 6x + 9.
Find the discriminant of 3x² + 2x − 1.
Solve 2x² − 5x − 3 = 0. What is the larger root?
How many real roots does x² + x + 1 = 0 have?
practice.sol: Δ = 1 − 4 = −3, which is negative, so there are no real roots.

quiz.why: The formula gives the same value for ±, so there is one repeated root.

quiz.q: What is the denominator of the quadratic formula?
quiz.why: It is 2a.

lessons.tip: Write a, b and c with their signs before substituting. Sign slips cause most errors.

lessons.title: Functions and graphs
goals: Use function notation f(x)
Find the gradient and intercept of a line
Find the vertex of a parabola
notes: A function gives exactly one output for each input. f(x) means "the output when the input is x".

notes.f: y = mx + c   (m = gradient, c = y-intercept)

notes: The graph of y = ax² + bx + c is a parabola. Its vertex is at x = −b / (2a). It opens upward if a > 0 and downward if a < 0.

examples.q: Find the equation of the line through (0, 1) and (2, 5)
steps: The line crosses the y-axis at 1

examples.q: Find the vertex of y = x² − 4x + 3

practice.q: If f(x) = 3x − 4, find f(5).
If f(x) = x² + 1, find f(−3).
Find the gradient of the line through (1, 2) and (4, 11).
What is the minimum value of y = x² − 6x + 5?
practice.sol: The vertex is at x = 3, so y = 9 − 18 + 5 = −4.

quiz.q: What is the y-intercept of y = −2x + 7?
quiz.why: In y = mx + c, the intercept is c = 7.
The coefficient of x² is negative.

lessons.tip: Sketch every answer. Even a rough graph catches sign errors.

lessons.title: Pythagoras and coordinate geometry
goals: Use Pythagoras' theorem
Find the distance and midpoint between two points
Test whether a triangle is right-angled
notes: In a right-angled triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides.

examples.q: The legs of a right triangle are 6 and 8. Find the hypotenuse.
Find the distance and midpoint of (1, 2) and (4, 6)

practice.q: A right triangle has legs 5 and 12. Find the hypotenuse.
The hypotenuse is 17 and one leg is 8. Find the other leg.
Find the distance between (−2, 1) and (4, 9).
Find the x-coordinate of the midpoint of (−2, 1) and (4, 9).

quiz.q: Is a triangle with sides 7, 24 and 25 right-angled?
options: Yes, because 25 is the longest side

quiz.why: Average the x-values and the y-values.

lessons.tip: Draw the right triangle under every coordinate-distance problem so students see where Pythagoras comes from.

lessons.title: Trigonometric ratios
goals: Name the opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse sides
Use sin, cos and tan to find sides
Recall the special-angle values
notes: Label the sides relative to the angle θ: opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse.
Memory aid: SOH CAH TOA.

examples.q: A 10 m ladder leans at 60° to the ground. How high up the wall does it reach?
steps: The height is opposite the 60° angle and the ladder is the hypotenuse

examples.q: The opposite side is 5 and the adjacent side is 5. Find the angle.

practice.q: A right triangle has opposite 6 and hypotenuse 10. What is sin θ?
A right triangle has adjacent 12 and hypotenuse 13. Find cos θ to 2 decimal places.
The hypotenuse is 20 and the angle is 30°. Find the side opposite the angle.
You stand 20 m from a tower and the angle of elevation to its top is 45°. How tall is the tower (m)?
practice.hint: Which ratio links opposite and adjacent?

practice.q: The hypotenuse is 14 and the angle is 60°. Find the adjacent side.

quiz.why: tan θ = opposite / adjacent.
This is one of the special-angle values.

lessons.tip: Make students label the triangle O, A and H before choosing a ratio.

lessons.title: Circles: length, area, arcs and sectors
goals: Find circumference and area
Find arc length and sector area
Choose a sensible value for π
notes: Use π ≈ 3.14 (or 22/7) unless the question says otherwise.
A sector is a "slice" of the circle, and θ is the angle at the centre.

examples.q: A circle has radius 7 cm. Use π = 22/7.
Find the arc length for a 90° sector with r = 8 (π = 3.14).

practice.q: Use π = 3.14. Find the area of a circle with radius 10.
Use π = 3.14. Find the circumference of a circle with diameter 20.
Use π = 3.14. Find the arc length of a 90° sector with radius 8.
Use π = 3.14. Find the area of a 60° sector with radius 6.

quiz.q: If the radius of a circle doubles, its area...
quiz.why: Area depends on r², and 2² = 4.

quiz.q: A semicircle is a sector with an angle of...
quiz.why: Half of 360° is 180°.

lessons.tip: Ask whether the answer needs units (length) or square units (area) before students write it down.

lessons.title: Laws of exponents
goals: Apply the laws of exponents
Work with zero, negative and fractional exponents
Simplify expressions with powers
notes: These laws only work when the bases are the same.

examples.q: Simplify 2³ × 2⁴
steps: Same base, so add the exponents: 2⁷

examples.q: Evaluate (3²)³

practice.q: Evaluate 5² × 5³ ÷ 5⁴.
Evaluate 2⁻³ as a decimal.
Evaluate 16^(1/2).
practice.sol: The exponent 1/2 means the square root: √16 = 4.

practice.q: Evaluate (x³)² × x⁻⁴ when x = 3.

quiz.why: Any non-zero number to the power 0 is 1.
Subtract the exponents: 5 − 2 = 3.

lessons.tip: Warn against "multiplying the bases": 2³ × 2⁴ is not 4⁷.

lessons.title: Sequences and series
goals: Find terms of arithmetic and geometric sequences
Sum an arithmetic series
Identify the common difference or ratio
notes: A sequence is an ordered list of numbers that follows a rule.

examples.q: Arithmetic sequence 3, 7, 11, … Find a₁₀ and S₁₀.
Geometric sequence 2, 6, 18, … Find a₅.

practice.q: Arithmetic sequence 5, 8, 11, … Find the 20th term.
Find the sum of the first 10 terms of 2, 4, 6, …
Geometric sequence 3, 6, 12, … Find the 6th term.
An arithmetic sequence has first term 4 and eighth term 25. Find the common difference.

quiz.why: Each term is multiplied by 2.

quiz.q: What is the common difference of 20, 17, 14, …?
quiz.why: Each term is 3 less than the one before.

lessons.tip: Ask: "Do I add the same number every time, or multiply by it?" before choosing a formula.

lessons.title: Logarithms
goals: Convert between exponential and logarithmic form
Use the product, quotient and power laws
Solve simple exponential equations
notes: A logarithm answers the question: "what power gives this number?"

list: log(a / b) = log a − log b

examples.q: Evaluate log₂ 32.
Solve 3ˣ = 81.

practice.q: Evaluate log₂ 64.
Evaluate log₁₀ 0.001.
Evaluate log₅ 125.
Evaluate log₂ 8 + log₂ 4.

quiz.why: This is the product law.

lessons.tip: Say it aloud: "log base 2 of 32 asks: 2 to what power is 32?"

lessons.title: Descriptive statistics
goals: Calculate the mean, median, mode and range
Choose the most suitable average
Find a missing value from a given mean

list: Mean = sum of values ÷ number of values
Median = middle value when sorted (average the two middle values if the count is even)

notes: Outliers pull the mean a lot, but barely move the median.

examples.q: Data: 4, 8, 6, 5, 3, 8. Find the mean, median, mode and range.
The mean of 5 numbers is 12. A sixth number makes the mean 13. Find it.

practice.q: Find the mean of 12, 15, 18, 20, 10.
Find the median of 7, 3, 9, 1, 5.
Find the median of 2, 4, 6, 8.
The mean of 6 numbers is 8. A 7th number makes the mean 9. Find the 7th number.
practice.sol: New total = 63, old total = 48, so the 7th number is 15.

quiz.q: A list of salaries has one very large outlier. Which average is most affected?
quiz.why: The mean uses every value, so a large outlier drags it up.
Sorted: 1, 1, 3, 4, 5. The middle value is 3 (2.8 is the mean).

lessons.tip: Always sort the data first. Most median errors come from skipping this step.

lessons.title: Probability basics
goals: Calculate simple probabilities
Use the complement, addition and multiplication rules
Work with independent events
notes: Probabilities lie between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain).

list: Mutually exclusive events: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)
Independent events: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)

examples.q: A fair die is rolled. Find P(even).
Two fair coins are tossed. Find P(both heads).

practice.q: A bag has 3 red and 5 blue balls. Find P(red) as a decimal or fraction.
A fair die is rolled. Find P(prime number).
practice.sol: The primes are 2, 3 and 5, so P = 3/6 = 1/2.

practice.q: Two fair dice are rolled. Find P(sum = 7) to 3 decimal places.
A fair coin is tossed and a die is rolled. Find P(head and a 6) to 3 decimal places.
A fair die is rolled. Find P(not a 6) to 3 decimal places.

quiz.q: If P(rain) = 0.3, what is P(no rain)?
Independent events A and B have P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.4. What is P(A and B)?

lessons.tip: Have students list the 36 outcomes of two dice once. It makes "6 ways to make 7" obvious.
